newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Latam leaders thank Peru for giving rebels lesson.
newsitem.headline: Latam leaders thank Peru for giving rebels lesson.

text.p: Latin American leaders on Wednesday hailed Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori for his daring solution to the Lima hostage crisis and prayed it would dissuade the region's guerrillas from similar escapades.

While human rights groups like Argentina's Mothers of Plaza de Mayo and Nobel Peace laureate Adolfo Perez Esquivel condemned the "spilling of the blood" of 14 Marxist rebels, national leaders breathed a sigh of relief.
"I would have acted the same way," said Fujimori's closest Latin American ally, Argentine President Carlos Menem, hailing the Peruvian leader's "spectacular courage."

Fujimori's regional colleagues thanked him for teaching a deadly lesson to the guerrillas who wage wars in many of their countries, hailing his decision to use force to free the 72 hostages held by Peruvian rebels since December.

But for the Mothers of Plaza de Mayo, who tried to mediate in Lima, the young Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels "died without killing, they died for others." Perez Esquivel said the Peruvian army "went into annhilate them."

Colombian President Ernesto Samper, whose country is racked by the violence of drug barons and guerrillas, said the rescue operation was "a warning to all terrorists in the world to understand that these methods gain nothing and just put their lives and others' lives at risk."
The government of Mexico's Ernesto Zedillo, who has his own rebel problem, condemned "acts of terrorism which put the lives of innocent people in danger and are never justified."
"Once more it is shown that violence only breeds violence," President Julio Sanguinetti of Uruguay, which saw some of Latin America's first urban guerrilla violence in the early 1970s, said.

"I hope this sad episode serves as a lesson never again to resort to violence in politics," said Sanguinetti, who angered Peru and Japan early in the crisis by freeing two suspected members of Peru's Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA).

Argentina, where the guerrilla violence of the 1970s triggered a brutal dictatorship in which up to 30,000 people were abducted and killed by the military, issued a statement praying the Lima crisis would "discourage any new escapades that do not coincide with our system of living in liberty."
For President Juan Carlos Wasmosy of Paraguay, who faced a military coup threat only one year ago, "this kind of decision was to be expected from a great statesman like Fujimori."

Most agreed with Fujimori that the deaths of one captive and two soldiers cast a cloud over the victory, but Chilean Foreign Minister Jose Miguel Insulza said Peru had little choice. "It must be recognised that after long and frustrating negotiations there were no alternatives to overcome the crisis in any other way," the Chilean diplomat said.
Venezuelan President Rafael Caldera said Peru's success "cannot eradicate the tragic history of this painful episode which I hope is never seen again in the history of America."

Bolivia's Gonzalo Sanchez de Lozada, hosting a summit of Andean presidents, saw fit to make a joke out of the situation late on Tuesday, saying: "Tomorrow we'll take someone hostage, possibly President Samper who wants to leave early."

There was also a note of caution from Menem that Fujimori had taken a very big risk. "Everything went fine. Everybody is applauding. If things had gone bad, they would have called him irresponsible," the Argentine leader said.
